summaries.summary: Active learning has received much interest for reducing annotation costs for text classification.
Active learning improves iteratively trained machine learning models by selecting unlabeled samples for annotation, with the number selected per iteration called the batch size.
Stopping methods are important for achieving active learning benefits in practice and have attracted substantial development interest.
Smaller batch sizes improve learning efficiency, but larger batch sizes improve development speed and ease of annotation, motivating analysis of batch size effects on a leading stopping method.
The authors evaluate batch size effects on active learning stopping methods for text classification using the publicly available 20Newsgroups dataset.
The base learner is a scikit-learn Support Vector Machine, with closest-to-hyperplane sampling, binary bag of words, words appearing more than three times, and a stop word list.
The Oracle Method stops at the first training iteration within a specified percentage of maximum achievable performance, with Oracle-99 set to 99 for contextualizing practical stopping results.
Experiments considered batch sizes of 1%, 5%, and 10% of the 20Newsgroups training data, summarized in Table~ SECREF4.
Oracle-99 needs more annotations with larger batch percents to reach approximately the same F-Measure as with smaller batch percents.
Results agree that larger batch sizes decrease learning efficiency, while raising whether stopping method parameters, especially window size, can reduce performance degradation.
BV2009 stops if the mean of the three previous kappa agreement values between consecutive models exceeds a threshold, and stops later than the optimal Oracle Method point for larger batch percents.
With window size of one, BV2009 stops with fewer annotations than with window size of three, without losing much F-Measure.
BV2009 requires INLINEFORM1 models before checking whether the average kappa agreement is above the threshold, marking its first possible stopping point.
Larger batch percents generate fewer models, and low early kappa agreement scores cause BV2009 to stop somewhat sub-optimally at very large batch percents.
Stopping methods degrade with larger batch sizes beyond learning efficiency losses, and smaller window sizes help mitigate this degradation.
This work was supported by The College of New Jersey SOSA program, MUSE program, and High Performance Computing System.
